text: Hi, Mitch. I'm one of the two co-founders of Basis. We are based right here in New York City, and the thing that we focus on is how can we get agents to do production-scale work reliably enough so that we are trusted and used end-to-end by accounting firms across the country. So a lot of our research really focuses on this. How can you get these agents to do real work in the real economy? So I want to maybe start with a question, which is, if you're at this conference, honestly, if you're watching this talk, you probably increase your own productivity a lot. You're using co-work or Codex or Cloud Code, whatever it is, and yet if you go look at the average company, the average enterprise, the average firm, their productivity hasn't gone up 10x, 100x. I know my productivity has gone up maybe 100x, but if I were working inside of a company, it wouldn't be anywhere near that order of magnitude. And so why is that? At Basis, one of the things we have is that humans are already used to working with non-deterministic systems. It's just those systems are normally their co-workers, not their computers. And so I actually think to answer this question, it's useful to maybe look at the existing way we organize intelligent systems, which are companies. So how do organizations scale their own productivity? Organizations need to trust that the people doing the work at every level are doing it in a way that is going to produce good outputs consistently at scale. If you look at this image here, here I'm showing an accounting firm, but this could honestly be any company, traditional company. The person who is the head of the firm, they have literally no idea about the exact day-to-day of the people at the very bottom. And yet somehow they trust the work is going to be done. How does that happen? It doesn't happen through deterministic systems, right? People are not deterministic. They're intelligent entities. And instead there are processes that are put in place, and those processes, if we believe the people who, you know, put them in place think that those processes will generalize to good outcomes, then they can be comfortable that even though the people executing the processes are not deterministic, you will generally get to good outcomes if you follow the process. This is true, by the way, even in the smallest steps. So in this example, earlier I was showing the process of maybe doing the monthly accounting work for a client at an accounting firm, but even within that process, say you wanted to see how do I reconcile the cash? Well, I need to get the bank data, and even that has a process. The process could be really basic. It could just be use the approved software to extract the data, but there's still some process that is put in place. You wouldn't expect the firm to just let anyone Google, you know, extract PDF and then just use whatever they want to go extract it, because now you wouldn't have process. Now let's talk about agents. As I said earlier, everyone already has CodeX, Cloud Code, but where is that productivity? Our opinion is there are two main problems that come with what I'll call coding style agent products where you're working with an agent and you just tell it to go and do something. The first problem is that there is a competency gap, because agents as you think of them as today, they outsource the complexity to the user. If I'm the user, I now have to manage my skill and memories and think about how to when I should use the agent. I have to have like theory of mind over it. This is really hard. And for those who are here, maybe you guys find it easy, but I promise for the wide majority of knowledge workers, they have no idea how to do any of this. And there's a second problem, which is there is a process gap, right? If you are saying, hey, user, here's your agent, do what you want, well, now suddenly the way the work is being done is essentially up to whoever the user is to customize the way the agent is behaving, which goes entirely against the way that organizations scale. The process should be coming from senior leadership down, not from any individual employee deciding how they're going to do their job, right? If you, going back to my example, if every employee just made up their own way of extracting data, you know, even back in 2018, that wouldn't be a good outcome. And so we believe strongly that the key to building production agents that actually do work end to end is solving these two problems. You have to solve the competency gap by making it simple. To the user, you shouldn't even have to know it's an agent, or you probably know, but you don't have to really feel it. It should be as simple as just working with a coworker. You just tell it what you want it to do, and all the things you expect to work should work. And the second is the process gap. You need agents to be reliable. Not having a stroke of genius one day and forgetting something the other day. It's not about being perfect. Humans are not perfect, right? Nobody is looking for perfect. What you're looking for is reliability and consistency and trustworthiness. So what does that actually look like? We think that to be simple and reliable, where you know you don't have to think about what to do, the agent can just do it for you without the user knowing the internals, to do it the same way consistently, you have to be opinionated. I just want to show you one slide back here. I want to point out that getting it right isn't actually the main task, because, again, humans are imperfect themselves. The point is to do it in a similar way. It's okay if you can't do something, but you should be consistently able to not do something, and then you get better, just like a person does. If you suddenly one day are an expert at something and then you miss something very basic that would be expected, now you're not reliable. So you have to be opinionated. What's an example of an opinion? Let's say we have an agent and we need to go and read a PDF. So in this case, what is the best way to read a PDF? There's many ways. You can throw it into a VLM, you can go write some Python code and use an open source OCR You can work with one of the many OCR-specific model providers. You could do an OCR and then you could have the VLM check its work. You could have five VLMs check its work. You could do 100 VLMs and take the best of N. There's literally infinite possibilities here. And so if you just said, agent, extract PDF, you might get good outcomes, but they're not going to be reliable. Not because the process it did was bad, but because the process it did was not opinionated. So the way we develop opinions is you use initial intuition, right? Some things you know what the opinions are from expertise. For example, if I'm trying to get an agent to do tax work well, I know that if the agent goes and reads the primary source before returning to the user, it is more likely to be accurate. I don't need a set of evals to tell me that. I don't need to divine that from first principles. We know that. Right? I know that if I have an agent make a PowerPoint, if it takes a picture of the PowerPoint before it returns to the user, it is less likely to have a formatting issue. That is obvious. And so there are lots of different ways to develop opinions. And one of the key points here I'll just make before I move on to talking about how to use the opinions, is that the opinions are not just about accuracy. Right? We just talked about the example of taking a picture of a PowerPoint. Well, that adds latency, right? You may not want that. Maybe the agent only makes formatting mistakes one out of a hundred times, and you're okay with that. And so therefore you don't have to take a picture of the PowerPoint. The point isn't exactly what the opinion is, and this talk we're going to focus not on how to develop opinions, but why opinions matter, and then how to leverage those opinions as you scale in production. So say you have a bunch of outcome-based evals. And when I say outcome-based evals, I mean what we traditionally think of as evals. It has a right answer. We have some rubric. We're trying to judge what the agent did. How do you know that the evals generalize to production? Right? You're going to have a thousand cases or a hundred cases, but in production, if you're doing real work, you're going to have hundreds of thousands of situations, and that's only going to increase as the trajectories get much longer, because the amount of decisions that are made in a trajectory just grow exponentially as the long-horizon abilities of agents increase. And so I can't prove, if you're looking at all these distribution of trajectories, you can't prove every one of them is correct. You don't have a ground truth for every trajectory. But you can potentially look at the trajectories to decide if the behavior, the opinion that you have, is actually happening. And you can then infer that if it's actually happening...
